utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. The case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I bid afternoon to all those present, the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused. We need to continue our work, but before we do that, on a procedural point. The last time I asked the Defence to let me know the list of documents for Witness BU. You asked me for a few days to think it over. I think that perhaps now you are in a position to let me know what those documents are. Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for reminding us. Yes, we have checked through the documents for this witness, and we do not have any documents to tender for Witness BU.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Nozica?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We also did not tender any documents for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have any documents for this witness. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Neither do we, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no documents to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, will you please rise so that you can take the solemn declaration. First, let me check that you're able to follow what I'm saying in your own language. If so, tell me, "I understand you."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please give me your first and last name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Fahrudin Agic. I was born on the 22nd of October, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your position or currents occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am a professional military man working in the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What rank do you have at present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a brigadier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you prefer us to address you as mister or using your grade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whichever you prefer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I will call you mister. Have you testified before in an international or national court of law about the events that took place in your country, or is this the first time for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is for me the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A second question: Within the framework of these proceedings, you have been interrogated by the investigators of the Prosecution. However, I want to ask you whether you have been questioned by investigators of your own country.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. You may be seated. Just some points of clarification: You have already met yesterday and maybe also this morning the Prosecutor, who I'm sure gave you some information about the way in which these proceedings will evolve. We will start with questions coming from the Prosecution, who is going to ask you questions about the events of 1992 and 1993 in the region of Prozor and Gornji Vakuf. It is also possible that the Judges in front of you at the bench may also ask you questions, either follow-up questions or in order to clarify certain points which we feel is necessary for a proper understanding of the events. The Prosecutor has envisaged to take the whole afternoon. Tomorrow, Wednesday, and Thursday, you will be asked to answer questions by the Defence counsels of the accused. You see that they are numerous. However, in fact there is one counsel per accused who will be asking you questions. It is possible, and I am quite sure that Mr. Praljak, who is an accused, who was also a high-ranking military officer, will also personally have some technical questions for you about those facts. We have granted the right to speak to General Praljak and General Petkovic, a minimum of one hour each. The rest of the time will be divided up by the other accused. You will note that the tone of the questions will change depending on the speakers. Normally, the Prosecutor will be addressing neutral questions, not leading questions, whereas the counsel of the accused will be asking you questions when you will sometimes be able to answer with a yes or no. The Judges have a different approach because we are seeking to establish the truth. We wish to have replies to legal and factual questions, and our approach is quite different, and you will realise that very quickly as we will be spending together three whole days. You're a high-ranking officer. You have a feeling for analysis and synthesis, so when answering a question, try and be precise, because as you know, in this field there is no place for approximations. Try and be precise so that the Judges who need to judge and rule about the relevance, reliability, and probative value of your words need to have a clear understanding of what is said. Should you have any difficulty in understanding the meaning of a question, sometimes these questions may be complicated, do not hesitate to ask the person asking you the question to reword it. You're a witness. You have rights and, above all, the right to understand a question. For technical reasons and in order to give the witnesses a chance to have a rest, we have a 20-minute break every hour and a half. If you have any health problems, please let us know and we can, of course, interrupt the proceedings whenever necessary. You will be able to comment on the documents that will be shown to you by one of the parties. These documents are those that you are probably familiar with, and I'm sure the Prosecutor has discussed them with you, and in this way we will be able to save some time. It is possible that during the cross-examination stage the questions could be difficult or sensitive, but please be calm. Don't get upset. The events that took place in your country are 13 years old, so to speak. Calmness is a necessity in this kind of process. So no dispute or conflict between the witness and the parties. Up to the present, as a general rule, everything was fine, and I believe it will continue to be so in your case. This is what I wanted to tell you before giving the floor to the Prosecution, who are going to begin their examination-in-chief. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor. Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Mundis begins his examination, I've just been asked to place on the record on behalf of all the Defence counsel the fact that yesterday at the close of proceedings, which would have been, I suppose, sometime after 6.00 in the evening, we were given a list of corrections to his statement made by the witness as a result of a proofing session. We just want to note that the original statement was made in February, 2000, and that we were only provided with these corrections after 6.00 yesterday evening. Bearing in mind the rulings made by the Trial Chamber in respect of previous witnesses, we do not make any formal objection to this, but we felt it right to place that fact on the record for the Trial Chamber's consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think that Mr. Mundis will probably respond, but I have been informed about this and I assume that yesterday afternoon the Prosecution reviewed the statement with the witness, the written statement, which was prepared on the 11th of February, 2000, and during the reading, word by word, paragraph by paragraph, the witness wished to make certain corrections, and that is why it was only at 6.00 p.m. that the Prosecution was able to inform the Defence of these alterations. Mr. Mundis, can you reassure Mr. Murphy with respect to this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Your Honour Judge Antonetti is absolutely correct. One thing that was slightly different with respect to this situation, that in the past was -- well, there are two factors. First of all, the original statement was taken in French and then translated into English and then translated from English into B/C/S. So there were two translation steps rather than the usual one. The witness indicated yesterday when he was reading the statement in his own language for the first time a number of corrections, and rather than trying to memorialise those in the form of a letter or a memo, it became obvious to the proofing team that the best way to proceed would be to do so by using the track changes technology that's available. So that's why it looks like a revised statement with what precisely was done in terms of additions, deletions, and corrections. I should also say for the benefit of everyone we did that in all three languages, although we were unable to provide the French version, I understand, until this morning. So there was additional delay in ensuring that the Bosnian-language and the English-language versions of this statement reflected all of the changes which the witness wished to make. So it was out of an abundance of caution and, of course, the Prosecution's desire to make sure that all the Defence teams have adequate access to all the material they need to prepare for cross-examination which resulted in this coming at this time in the day rather than perhaps a little bit earlier, when we could have done that in the form of a memo. But quite frankly, that would have been confusing because the English version of the statement did not have paragraph numbers. So it was -- would have been extremely difficult and perhaps confusing to have done so in any other way than the way we chose to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis, for this explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Brigadier Agic.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to start by asking you just a few brief questions concerning your background. Sir, where are you from?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I'm from Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And were you living in Gornji Vakuf at the time the war started?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was born in Ploce. I lived up till 1983 in the village of Trnovaca and moved to Gornji Vakuf, a part of the town known as Kosuta.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what were you doing prior to the war? How were you employed?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Before the war I was employed in the Territorial Defence as Chief of Staff for the municipality of Gornji Vakuf. And again let's focus on early 1992. Did you have any rank or what were your primary responsibilities in the Territorial Defence as Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Up until April, I was Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was part of Yugoslavia. When Bosnia and Herzegovina gained independence, the state authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina decided to form the Territorial Defence of the Independent Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as of the first multi-party elections, the HDZ got the position of Staff Commander. Then the Assembly relieved me of the position of Chief of Staff and appointed to that position Mr. Mladen Kovacevic, and I was appointed to the position of Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us approximately when this change occurred, when you were relieved and Mr. Mladen Kovacevic was appointed.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: This was the beginning of April, and it was decided at an Assembly meeting. The Assembly is the highest body of the socio-political community in those days, and the Assembly was entitled to do this with the approval of the senior command, that is, the District Staff of the TO in Zenica. When the new TO was formed, we were given a form with a statement of the minister of defence. His name was Jerko Doko. And we had to fill in this form to state our loyalty to the new TO Staff of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did you, sir, in fact complete this loyalty form?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I filled in this form, and most of the people in the staff, with the exception of those people who were Croats by ethnicity. I think perhaps Luka Sekerija was a Croat who signed this loyalty form, but as far as I can remember, this was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, again, sir, in the period April, 1992, what was the approximate strength of the TO in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: In the old TO there was a total of 2.000, including units in work organisations and local communities. But according to the new structure, the TO numbered 1.600 men in the month of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you inform us as to the approximate breakdown of that 1.600-man TO in Gornji Vakuf in terms of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Almost 100 per cent were Bosniaks, with the exception of a few cases. We had two officers of Serb ethnicity and a third officer of Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the commander, Mladen Kovacevic. How long did he remain as the commander of the TO in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: He remained until about mid-May, between the 15th and 20th of May when he definitely left the TO. And Musa Fikret was appointed in his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, for the benefit of the transcript, when you refer to between 15th and 20th of May, what year was that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: It was 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At that point in time, did Mladen Kovacevic join any other military organisation?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: At first he didn't, but I think in October, 1992, he joined the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge can you tell us when the HVO was formed in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I heard that for the first time at a joint meeting at the end of April and the beginning of May when we were discussing the formation of units and preparations. That was the first time for me to see the HVO insignia. Pero Mejdandzic was wearing it and he introduced himself as Chief of Staff of the HVO TO for Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, we have to be absolutely clear. What year was this when you had the joint meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why were you having this joint meeting? What was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: The purpose of the meeting was for us to try and form joint armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: To prepare for the struggle against aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to intervene, but it seems that there is an important mistake in the transcript. The gentleman said that Pero Mejdandzic represented HVO of Gornji Vakuf and the transcript said TO. That is line 23 on page 10. I think that should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I thank my colleague for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, there appears to be an error in the transcript, Brigadier Agic. Can you tell us, Pero Mejdandzic was appointed the Chief of Staff of what military formation in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: He introduced himself as the Chief of Staff of the HVO for Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know how long he remained in that position?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I think he remained until August, and then Mr. Zrinko Tokic took over from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I think we're going to have a recurring problem here, sir. If at any time you indicate a month if you could also tell it us the year that would be very helpful. When did Mr. Tokic take over?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I think it was in beginning -- it was at the beginning of August, 1992, or perhaps the end of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And throughout this period, again now we're focusing from April, 1992, until towards the end of 1992, what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Until the 10th of August, I held the position I was appointed to and that is Chief of Staff. And on the 10th of August, I became commander of the Municipal Staff of the TO for Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During this period, again from April, 1992, through the summer of 1992, can you characterise the relationship between the TO in Gornji Vakuf and the HVO in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: In May we formed a joint line, one next to the other, in the region of Radusa towards the front held by the army of Republika Srpska towards Kupres. As far as possibilities allowed, we endeavoured to fortify those lines jointly. However, a number of factors had their effect, and above all the problem of the use of communications, also supplies, so that these problems increased. There were certain incidents that occurred which reached a climax on the 20th of June, because on that date -- or, rather, the 19th of June, 1992, there was an armed clash between members of the Territorial Defence and the HVO in Novi Travnik. As these are two neighbouring municipalities, this had repercussions on Gornji Vakuf. I need to point out that between the 15th and the 20th, a unit arrived from Croatia in the region of Gornji Vakuf. The unit was known as Garavi. It numbered between 60 and 65 members, and on the 19th or the 18th of June, 1992, the Frankopani unit was deployed in Gornji Vakuf, and the commander, with members of his command, were put up in the hotel where the unit was put up, in the secondary school centre and in the department store. On the 20th of June, 1992, in the afternoon, between 1440 and 1500 hours, the HVO from the lower part of the town opened fire on the part of the town inhabited by majority Muslim population. In the meantime, the unit Garavi in location Karamustafic set up a check-point and started arresting and taking people to a meadow that had a wire fence around it, and that is where people were stopped, searched, identified, and held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have to intervene at this point. You have just said that there was a so-called Garavi unit that arrived in the Gornji Vakuf area, and you added that this unit apparently came from Croatia. Can you provide us with any additional information that would allow us to identify the origin of this Garavi unit? Did they have vehicles, uniforms, insignia? Why were they there? Was there an agreement according to which they were to cooperate in military terms with some other body? Could you add any other information to what you have just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what the commander of that unit, called Klica, who was older than me, two years older than me, and I knew him personally since we had gone to the same school, he was from Vilic Polje, when I spoke to him according to what he said well he came from Pakrac. He mentioned fighting in that area of Croatia. He mentioned the structure of the unit. He said the unit was composed of soldiers who had voluntarily left Bosnia and Herzegovina to go to war in Croatia. They had been gathered or assembled in the unit. They had fought in Croatia as the Garavi unit. They all had ID cards from the Croatian army and on their sleeves most of them had Croatian army insignia, whereas on their other sleeve they had the Garavi insignia. This was a unit that was in Vakuf quite frequently. After the Washington agreement, General Roso personally ordered they should leave the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so they then returned to Kupres in 1995, and their commander lost a leg there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I have understood your testimony, this so-called Garavi unit had been composed or assembled in Croatia. They were -- they were composed of men who had come from Bosnia-Herzegovina, men who had gone to Croatia and who were volunteers within that unit. Is that in fact what you are telling us? And all the more so because you said you knew their commander because you went to school with that person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite right. That's exact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they arrived in the Gornji Vakuf area, in the surroundings of Gornji Vakuf, but what was the purpose of their arrival there? Why was it necessary for them to be there at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the pretext was that they had come to prepare for fighting in the direction of Kupres. The commander of the Frankopan unit, Zulu, also said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said it was the pretext. Was that the purpose or the pretext? Mr. Karnavas is shaking his head, because he's wondering about this just like myself. Was it the pretext or was it the objective? Was the objective to go and fight in Kupres, or did they say, "We're here to fight around Kupres, but in fact we have another purpose in mind"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, time showed that that was a pretext. They had come to take control of Gornji Vakuf. On that day in the afternoon, the Garavi unit took control of the entrance to Gornji Vakuf at the juncture for the roads to Dobrasin-Karamustafic, because there's only one house there. It's not a settlement. They took over the road there in order to control the passage of people in both directions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question: If I have understood you correctly, a foreign unit came to put up check-points, to establish control over the surroundings of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Brigadier Agic, you also mentioned a few moments ago the Frankopani unit. Do you know the strength of that formation?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Between 300 and 350 well-equipped troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me go back, sir, to the period of time in the spring and summer of 1992 when you and the HVO or the TO and the HVO were jointly defending the line against the VRS. How closely were you working with Zrinko Tokic during that time period?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: We had daily contact initially in terms of -- well, in military terms, and we cooperated in the area where we had to establish the line. We tried to fill in certain gaps in the lines. The HVO also provided certain materiel, certain supplies. We would receive fuel that we paid for. We also received some of the uniforms from them, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on this daily contact, did you become familiar with the structure of the HVO in terms of how the HVO in Gornji Vakuf fit into a larger structure?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Well, in Gornji Vakuf the HVO established a brigade with three battalions. Vakuf is not a large town. The municipality isn't very large either. We all knew each other, and some of the officers who were in the Territorial Defence, those who were of Croatian nationality, joined the Ante Starcevic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where was the Ante Starcevic Brigade headquartered?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: The headquarters were located in the factory, in the textile factory called Yassa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for the record Yassa is in what town?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Yassa is in an area of Gornji Vakuf called Bistrica. It's west of the Novi Travnik-Gornji Vakuf road. It's about 4 to 500 metres to the west of that road. It's in the vicinity of the village of Batusa. There was only the Vrbas between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, as a result --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Vrbas River.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As a result of your contact with Zrinko Tokic, the HVO Brigade commander in Gornji Vakuf, did you become aware of to whom he reported?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Apart from myself, Zrinko mostly had contact with the then commander, Musa Fikret, commander of the ABiH. But I know that his immediate superior was in Duvno or rather, in Tomislavgrad. That's the operation's zone of Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who was the commander of the operation zone Tomislavgrad in mid-1992?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I do. When we said we needed something, he had to obtain approval to take action. He had to receive approval from the commander of the Tomislavgrad operative zone and that was Colonel Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you know, sir, based upon your dealings with the HVO command, local HVO command, to whom Colonel Siljeg reported as the operation zone Tomislavgrad commander?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that in May, but I knew that the HVO headquarters was in Grude. Later, I found out that the person concerned was General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what time period was General Petkovic the person concerned at the HVO headquarters in Grude?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I know that General Petkovic was there from August onwards. I don't know if he was there prior to that date as a commander of the HVO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Brigadier Agic, a few questions about the structure of the TO at this point in time, that is mid-1992.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: You told us that there were 1.600 men in the TO in Gornji Vakuf; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the materiel in terms of weaponry that was available to the Gornji Vakuf TO in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: When I said they'd had 1.600 men, according to the structure in place at the time -- well, it was what we called a formation, what the soldiers would call a formation. In October and after, October they started forming brigades, and then a brigade was formed in Gornji Vakuf that consisted of 2.560 men. It was a Mountain Brigade according to its establishment. Initially we would buy weapons from smugglers who had come from the Republic of Croatia, from arms traffickers and other dealers who'd pass through Gornji Vakuf, who would come to Gornji Vakuf. And we also used some hunting weapons, the hunting weapons that citizens of Gornji Vakuf had, those who were members of the sporting society, hunting society, since hunting is a very popular sport in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President. The witness did not directly answer the question posed to him, and I think this is going to be a problem. I know that Mr. Mundis is asking very precise questions because he wishes to get very precise answers. So perhaps the gentleman could be asked to answer the question, because I think the -- how this TO progressively goes from 1.600 to 2.500, what weapons they had back in May and onwards may become an issue that is important to all of us here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you add other information with regard to the Territorial Defence, but there's a question that one should have immediately put to you. In 1993 -- or, rather, 1992, you were 34 years old. I've come to the conclusion that you must have done your military service when you were between 20 and 25 years old. Did you serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't. I was -- I worked in the TO defence in -- from 1980 onwards, after I had done my military service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So where did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I served in the military in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when you left, did you have a rank? Were you just a private, a non-commissioned officer, an officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Staff Commander, that's the position individuals are assigned to. There's an establishment rank that is allocated. In peacetime this didn't mean much since Territorial Defence members did not have any uniforms, but according to the rank I had, I was a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, the gentleman attended what would be a school for reserve officers, not a regular military academy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you served in the military in a reserve school, not in a military academy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And there was also training provided in the Territorial Defence units. That training was provided in the former system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis, it would be good for the Judges to have more information with regard to the Territorial Defence. If you could put a series of questions to the witness so that everyone could be provided with the appropriate information. I could do it myself, but I would rather you proceeded in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Brigadier Agic, at the time the TO had 1.600 men in the spring of 1992, how many weapons did the TO in Gornji Vakuf have?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: The TO in Gornji Vakuf at the time period you're interested in, March to April, had between 200 and 300 pieces -- 200, 300 weapons, military weapons, obtained from various sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you describe for us, sir, the structure of the TO from the level of the Municipal Staff in Gornji Vakuf up the chain of command to where the ultimate authority or responsibility for the TO rested? Again, I'm talking about the summer -- spring and summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: According to the initial formation in Gornji Vakuf, we were the TO Defence Staff of the third variant. According to that variant, the TO in Gornji Vakuf had 1.600 men who in three Territorial Defence detachments. There was a logistics base, there was a police platoon, and there was an Officers Staff Command of the TO. We had a subordinate command, and our First Superior Command was located in Zenica. There was a District Staff of the TO in Zenica that was established then. Zenica was subordinate, and its superior body was the Republican Staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The commander of the TO in Zenica was Colonel Ramiz Suvalic at the time, and the commander of the Republican Staff was Colonel Hasan Efendic. The minister of defence was Mr. Jerko Doko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention now, Brigadier Agic, to the period when the TO was transformed toward the latter part of the 1992. Do you recall when this transformation began?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a follow-up question. The 1.600 men who were members of the TO, of the Territorial Defence, what status did they have? Did they have the status of members of the military? Were they civilians who had provisionally been mobilised or who were serving for a period in the Territorial Defence? Could you provide us with some information concerning the status of TO members? In one word, were they members of the military? Were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They were soldiers who had reported or, rather, through the defence secretariat they'd been assigned to TO units, and they started doing their military service. At the end of May, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina issued an order on general mobilisation, mobilisation of men and of equipment in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a -- I'll provide you with an example I have in mind right now, but if a villager says that he is a member of the TO, should one draw the conclusion, as you seem to be saying, that if that is what he says, he is necessarily a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He's deployed in the TO through a state body, the municipal staffs of the TO state administrative bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As a point of clarification, Your Honour, the gentleman said military service. That was on page 21, line 11. Prior to the formation of the ABiH one would do their military obligation, not service, with the Territorial Defence. Perhaps the gentleman wishes to correct me if I'm -- if I'm incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When a citizen served in the Territorial Defence, was such a citizen a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. The Territorial Defence was an integral part of the defence system in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and these were the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the beginning. The army hadn't been established at that time. That's why I'm saying they were soldiers, because they had been assigned to TO units as citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was their duty to carry out the tasks assigned to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be more precise, at the time of the former Yugoslavia, the JNA was in fact the army. When the JNA had withdrawn, was replaced by the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The State of Bosnia-Herzegovina only took over the system of defence that was already in existence, because the Republican Staff of the SFRY that had existed up until then was transformed, and instead of that term we had the Territorial Defence Staff of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But the system was taken over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, those who are members of the TO, as far as we have understood, after the order issued by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, these people were soldiers. I'd like a clarification. What did the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina have to say with regard to all the men who were between 16 and 60 years of age? Were they automatically members of the Territorial Defence and, therefore, soldiers, or were men who had been recruited in fact the men who were members of the Territorial Defence, and only these men who had been recruited. So my question concerns people between the age of 16 and 60 years of age.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In April men from 16 to 60 weren't mobilised. Members of the Territorial Defence were people who had served or men who had served in the former JNA, so they were military-able men, able-bodied men. Not all citizens were members of the TO. Only those fit to perform their military service were such members. That was the case until all the units had been brought up to establishment strength. They would then be given a wartime assignment by the defence department from the ministry of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We called that the defence secretariat or the municipal defence secretariat at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: May I say a few words. Frankly, I do not understand why the question of the TO has taken so much time away from the Prosecution. I believe that at this Tribunal it is quite clear that the TO was a part and parcel of the national defence of the former Yugoslavia, and as the witness now explained, the able-bodied men who were already in the army, the JNA, they then become, in general, party to the TO. And of course it has been the previous system and it probably remained so during the first months of the independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. Afterwards when the general mobilisation entered into force, then of course the -- the TO had to be reorganised and to be, I would say, based on -- on the -- on those other persons who had joined the TO. But again, I say that I do not see too much controversy here, but -- and therefore I would say that we may go on from this issue and to let the Prosecution to continue actually it's examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you share the conclusion made by the Judge of the Chamber regarding what has just been said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but I feel it might be useful at this stage already to explain. On the 8th of April, 1992, the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, issued a decree abolishing the Republican Staff of the TO and forming TO staffs of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And it follows from this that this was not a question of the continuity of the TO but a new organisation being established which only retained the name of TO. And I think that we will be able to find out that two months later, that is in August, 1992, the decision was taken that the TO should be replaced with the words, "the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina," so that this was a continuity of armed forces with different names rather than parallel existence of two military organisations, one being the army and the other the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence, and more specifically Ms. Alaburic, submits, and your opinion is important in this connection, that after the 8th of April, 1992, there was no continuity of the TO in the sense as it existed in the ex-Yugoslavia but in fact a new entity which was formed as the army. What do you think about this? Was this a continuity, or was it a real change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just said what the lady repeated. The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in April set up a new Bosnian TO, if I can call it that. And I said that we were given statements to sign by the defence -- from the Defence Minister that in future the members of this new Bosnian army should sign. And the lady is quite right. Afterwards, this led to the formation of the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you just mentioned this led to the formation of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: The preparation started in the month of August, but the real proper units of the Bosnian army were formed in the area I'm talking about. In Sarajevo this may have taken place earlier, but in the area of Central Bosnia the preparations to form the 3rd Corps started in August onwards, and it was finally formed in October. Then came the formation of brigades, the personnel, and so on, but the structure of an army in the process of formation cannot be achieved quickly and efficiently under conditions of a shortage of resources, a lack of unity of territory, complications regarding control and command, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Once this transformation from the TO to the ARBiH occurred, what happened to the TO Staff in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: TO staffs required a new role according to the defence law passed at the time, and this was that they became military territorial bodies which would serve and logistically assist the TO brigades as the operational units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the TO Staff that you were with in Gornji Vakuf, did it assume a new identity as part of this transformation?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: It was called the defence staff of the municipality. The word "territorial" was redacted. But they were abolished for good at the end of September. All the functions of these staffs were taken over by brigade commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And Gornji Vakuf, what brigade command assumed the functions formerly held by the TO Staff?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: By order of the state Presidency, the Mountain Brigade was formed in Gornji Vakuf, and it was called the 317th, and it was part of the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where was the headquarters of the 3rd Corps of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: The command was in Zenica. I think in the building of the ironworks there. I think it was known as the engineering works or building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the strength upon its formation of the 317th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: It was a Mountain Brigade, and it numbered 200, 560 [as interpreted] men with three battalions. An anti-armour company, 120-millimetre mortar company, and a logistics company, and a military police company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you -- can you repeat -- can you repeat the numbers? It didn't seem to be recorded accurately in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you repeat that? We don't seem to be getting --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain for the Trial Chamber how it was that the TO in the spring had 1.600 men yet in the fall the 317th Mountain Brigade had 2.560 men?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: This is -- this has a simple explanation, because we know that the formations were changed. The most important thing was for the defence secretariat to have sufficient number of men of -- able-bodied men to join the armed forces. So that through the Secretariat of National Defence or Defence, the additional men were assigned to these brigades in addition to those who belonged to the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what was the source of these additional men that were assigned to the brigades? Where did these men come from?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: From the territory of Gornji Vakuf municipality. And a smaller number of people joined who in fled from the area of Kupres, Jajce, Donji Vakuf. But that number is negligible in relation to the total. For a while in Gornji Vakuf, there were some 30 men from Modrica, and in August we sent them to Zenica. They came from the area of Modrica. And when Bosanski Brod fell, I don't know how, but they managed to reach Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Brigadier Agic, that the date that the 317th Mountain Brigade was established?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: The 17th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, sir, at the time the 317th Mountain Brigade was established what the relationship was between that unit and the HVO Brigade in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: You mean in the month of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: They were very strained and difficult. It was difficult to achieve communication with them. In those days, we even tried and finally succeeded in limiting our communications to those through UNPROFOR. If we had any disagreements, it was via UNPROFOR that we got in touch with each other and agreed as to the ways we should proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this stage you're telling us that the Brigade was formed on the 17th of October, 1992. And 2.560 men, did they have a uniform with a badge indicating the 317th Brigade. The officers, commander, the Chief of Staff, did they have stamps with the indication "Bosnia-Herzegovina, 3rd Corps, 317th Brigade"? In brief, this 317th Brigade, was it a real unit or a virtual unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 17th is the date of the establishment of the brigade, but this is a process that had to take time. They didn't have uniforms. The officers did have uniforms. At first we didn't have any brigade insignia, but all members of the brigade did receive the insignia of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the command officers had what we called "wartime ranks" indicating the position the person held. They were in yellow or green depending on the service that person belonged to, the person wearing this sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how long, sir, did it take for the 317th Mountain Brigade to constitute itself as a -- as a real military unit with uniforms and ranks and adequate supplies, et cetera? How long did this process take?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: That didn't depend only on us who were in Gornji Vakuf. This was a broader problem when talking about units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Supplies were a problem. Logistics were a problem. So from the month of April, we managed quite quickly to complete the manning, but the rest regarding the establishment of a real brigade was quite a problem. There was a shortage of uniform, weaponry, and other equipment that goes with a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time the 317th Mountain Brigade was established, what position or function did you hold?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I was Chief of Staff of the defence. The commander was Jusuf Delic, because he was the highest ranking person in the former Territorial Defence. He had the rank of major. And his deputy was Captain First Class Adem Kilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Brigadier Agic, when you became a member of the 317th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I was appointed commander. I think it was the 5th of October, 1993, after Mr. Enver Zejnalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what position did you hold from October, 1992, until the 5th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I was Staff Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Of what unit?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: The Defence Staff for Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a few words could you define the qualities of a chief of staff and the duties of the Chief of Staff of a brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A brigade Chief of Staff? The duties of a chief of staff, he's head of the staff. He's in charge of the staff, and he takes care of planning, the deployment of units, and the functioning of all the services engaged in planning, and he replaces the commander in his absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, a few moments ago, as reflected on -- I believe it was page 28, lines 3 and 4, you told us that relations between the 317th Mountain Brigade and the HVO were strained in Gornji Vakuf and difficult. Can you elaborate upon that? What do you mean by "strained," and perhaps give us an example.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I could give you several examples. The situation in Central Bosnia at the time was, let me say, highly confusing or chaotic. In October, there was another armed conflict in Novi Travnik which affected the situation in Gornji Vakuf very seriously, so that it was difficult to communicate, and the capture of positions, the deployment of units, et cetera. In October there was an open conflict in the region of Prozor, and Prozor was militarily captured and taken by the HVO, and all this was reflected upon Gornji Vakuf. And in the evening of the 20th and 21st of October, there was an exchange of fire in town, and the HVO fired several projectiles on the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, prior to this incident on the 20th and 21st of October, 1992, were there any other incidents in Gornji Vakuf that strained relations between the Croats and the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I already mentioned the exchange of fire on the 20th of June. There were also some casualties. And in the course of that month there were other incidents in the region of Vojica, again with several dead. During the summer at a Croat HVO check-point next to the clothing factory Borac, vehicles were stopped belonging to the TO who were bringing back shifts from Radusa. These were disarmed, and in one case these weapons were never returned. More than 20 pieces were seized. And we had cases when a soldier of ours would be beaten up and physically mistreated, and all this further complicated the situation. And the situation in Novi Travnik was reflected on the situation in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's me draw your attention, Brigadier Agic, to the 16th of October, 1992. Do you remember any particular incidents on that day?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: An incident involving a flag?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. On that day, the civilian police was put up in the Radusa hotel. Close to that hotel is a crossroads of roads leading to Bugojno, Novi Travnik, and the centre of town. An HVO soldier came carrying a black Ustasha flag with a big letter U with the words: "Ready to Die for the Fatherland" on it. And where normally flags are hoisted on holidays, he hung up that flag. And the policeman from the MUP of Gornji Vakuf removed that flag, and while he was doing so, members of the HVO opened fire from the post office and wounded this policeman. After that, in the town of -- centre where the lines were from the beginning and remained there, there was an exchange of fire on both sides. So that during the night Mr. Zrinko and myself and other senior officers, whose duty it was to take steps, did efforts to avoid any escalation, and by the morning we managed to calm the situation down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Brigadier Agic, a few moments ago you mentioned the town of Prozor. Can you tell us what happened in Prozor in the autumn of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, could we have some foundation? Is this from what he heard, or was he there personally? Which of the two? And also, I might add when he was asked to give examples, I failed to hear any examples where Muslim may have acted in provocative ways that would have strained relations. Are we to consider that there were no acts on their part?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I think that's certainly a subject that can be covered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Incident with the flag, were you present there or you were told about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in town, and I reached the spot in five minutes. Vakuf is a small town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you arrived there five minutes later; is that right? To the best of your recollection, do you remember incidents where Croats were not opposed to Muslims but the other way around, when Muslims provoked Croats? Do you remember any such incidents or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I am aware of such incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us one by way of an example so that there should be a balance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an event at the beginning of June when a member of the TO from Grnica, his surname is a Grizic, forget his first name, in the village of Bistricka Rijeka, which is on the way to Novi Travnik, he stopped a husband and wife of Croatian ethnicity, looted them, tied their hands behind their backs with wire, and killed them in a most brutal fashion. That event worsened the situation, but in 24 hours we found the perpetrator. And, instead of the situation calming down, it got worse, because the HVO wanted us to hand them over -- hand him over to him [as interpreted], for the -- him to be taken to trial in Mostar, but we didn't agree to that. We sent him to Zenica, and that person was sentenced to 20 years in prison. And he's still serving his term. But incidents of this kind could get the situation quite out of hand. And this occurred on a daily basis. The TO forces and the secured forces, everyone was involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that in this particular incident that the perpetrator Grizic was sent to Zenica where apparently he was tried and sentenced, and apparently he's still in prison. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, we're coming close to the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I was going to suggest we take the break at this point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll take a 20-minute break and we'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Brigadier Agic, I wanted to return to a subject that you mentioned earlier this afternoon reflected on page 13, line 4. You mentioned a check-point at the Karamustafic location. Other than that check-point were there at any point in time in 1992 other check-points established in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: From May or June onwards there were check-points that had been set up on -- in -- because of certain agreements and there were people who took the initiative and set up check-points. The Karamustafic check-point had been agreed on. That was also the case for the Humac and Devec check-points. Those check-points were set up, and they were manned by military police members from the HVO and the Territorial Defence and later the armija. After every incident, the HVO would set up additional check-points. In Trnovaca, in Krupa, and near Borac. It's the industrial zone, the entrance to Gornji Vakuf when you come from the direction of Bugojno. And this was also done in the village of Dobrasin near the so-called Krecana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you just told us that after every incident the HVO would set up additional check-points. What were you referring to when you said "after every incident"?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I was referring to incidents that brought the situation to a head and as a result of the risk of fire being opened. Whenever someone opened fire, check-points would be established at the locations I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what do you mean by additional HVO check-points, the HVO would set up additional check-points? Where would they do this?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I've just said that they set up check points the village of Trnovaca. That was a check-point that hadn't been agreed upon. And they set up a check-point in the industrial zone, in the village of Krupa and in Dobrasin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was it possible to pass through these check-points for Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: It depended on those who had set up the check-points. Usually the men who were found or the people who were found at the check-points would be taken in. Their property would be stolen. Some of them would also be beaten up. And after things had calmed down these people would usually be released and return to the places they had come from but without their property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Before the break we were about to talk about Prozor. Let me ask you this: In the autumn of 1992, were you in Prozor at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: No. I hadn't been in Prozor since July. The first time I went there afterwards, after the fall of Prozor, was on the 23rd of October, I believe. I went there with Colonel Mandic [as interpreted], and we visited Mejnik, Glibe, Jurici, Slijme [phoen]. Our intention was to calm the situation down and inspect the area, to ensure that there were no armed units on either side. And I didn't go to Prozor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who is Colonel Mandic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Antic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. So we need to correct that in the transcript. Who is Colonel Antic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Andric. I met Mr. Andric at the beginning of October in Gornji Vakuf. We had dinner in the restaurant. At the time it was a discotheque at Sandro. He introduced himself as the commander of an area under the control of the HVO. It was from Colakovic, Bijelo Polje, and onwards towards Rudnik. That's the area that he controlled. That's how he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was the purpose for you and Colonel Andric to go to Prozor? Why? What prompted you to go there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: At a suggestion made by UNPROFOR -- well, as I said, when Prozor fell, that evening fire was opened in Vakuf by both parties. UNPROFOR then suggested that we should go to the area that I have just mentioned. I accepted the suggestion, and I arrived at the Prozor command under HVO escort. We had a meeting, had a coffee, and visited the area around Mejnik. We inspected the area, spoke to the people, the civilians who lived there. We then returned to Prozor. And I had to go to Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did you receive any information about what had happened in Prozor and, if so, from whom?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I knew more or less what had happened in Prozor because I was made aware of it through the chain of command. When I was in Prozor, I saw what the situation was like. There had been armed clashes in the area of Mejnik. So I gained a fuller picture of what had happened in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the date that, as you put it, Prozor fell?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it was on the 21st of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And after -- on or about the 21st of October, 1992, what force was in control in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: The town of Prozor itself, the entire town and part of the municipality of Prozor, in the direction of Tomislavgrad, and also in the direction of Jablanica and the village of Here. It was under the control of the HVO. I realised this when I went to the commission that was supposed to see what had happened. I went with Mr. Tokic Zrinko, because we were supposed to attend the meeting and to make an attempt to calm the situation down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you mean by the commission that was supposed to see what happened?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Well, at that meeting the meeting should have been attended by the following as ordered by the commander, I suppose: On may have of the army, armija, there was General Arif Pasalic; the commander of the Bugojno TO Staff, Senad Dautovic; myself, the TO commander from Gornji Vakuf; on behalf of the HVO, Colonel Zeljko Siljeg was supposed to attend the meeting; and Juergen or Jure Schmidt. Colonel Siljeg didn't attend the meeting. He said he had been prevented from doing so. And on behalf of the HVO, the meeting was attended by Juergen Jure Schmidt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, a question -- Colonel, a question. You said that Prozor fell on the 21st of October, and then apparently there was a meeting with General Pasalic, Dautovic, et cetera. You're quite sure that it was on the 21st of October? Because in the indictment it says that it was on the 23rd of October. So are you quite sure it was on the 21st of October, or is this a date that you're not a hundred per cent sure about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not a hundred per cent sure of that. I was born on 22nd of October. I know I was in Jablanica after my birthday. I was in Jablanica at this meeting, and the meeting was held two days after Prozor had been taken, so that's how I came to this date. But you may be quite right. It may have been on the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you say that your birthday is on the 22nd. Everyone remembers their birthday. There can be no mistakes there. So the fall of Prozor was, in your opinion, prior to your birthday or after your birthday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think it was on the 21st of October, as I have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, after Prozor fell, what steps, if any, were taken by the 317th Mountain Brigade or the TO Staff in Gornji Vakuf with respect to the defence of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Two steps were taken. A third battalion -- or, rather, the 2nd Battalion in Voljevac was ordered to take up positions in the area of the village of Pridvorci in order to prevent an HVO breakthrough in that area or sector. And we spend the entire day in the town trying to calm the situation down, and by evening we had managed to take control of the situation and to ensure that both sides stopped clashing. Unfortunately, certain people were killed, but by the end of the day we had managed to calm things down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What steps, sir, if any were taken in terms of fortifying the town or preparing defence lines around the town?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: In the town and around the town nothing was done to fortify the lines, absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: We weren't expecting a clash with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us how the situation progressed in the months of November and December, 1992, in the town of Gornji Vakuf with respect to relations between the ARBiH and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: During this period we tried to get back to normal. We were mostly concerned with the lines in the direction of Kupres. However, during this period of time, the Serbian forces took control of Jajce. There was a lot of troop movement on the roads. As for Vakuf, the HVO tried to increase the strength of its units every day. So at the end of November, there were quite a lot of uniformed men in Vakuf, men who weren't from Gornji Vakuf. This caused the men and soldiers to be afraid. So given that the HVO was increasing the strength of its units in Gornji Vakuf, the situation became more tense and the relationship aggravated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What steps were taken, if any, as a result of the increase in the strength of HVO units in Gornji Vakuf in November, December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: The brigade and the staff informed the 3rd Corps about all these events. General Hadzihasanovic issued an order stating that brigade and staff units should do all they could to avoid a conflict. Attempts were made to avoid such a conflict at all costs, but often people's property was stolen on roads, people arrested, taken in, and this compounded the situation on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'd like to clarify something that you said a while ago. You said that in Gornji Vakuf there was the HVO and they were increasing the strength of their units, and you said that these people weren't local people. They had come from elsewhere apparently. So the HVO men who went to Gornji Vakuf, as far as you know, in your opinion, which area had they come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I assume that they had come from the area of Livno and Duvno and from Western Herzegovina. Gornji Vakuf is a very small town. When strangers appear in town this is immediately noticed. And these men acted in a very arrogant and brazen way, and there were provocations in the town itself, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In military terms, you're a general, so you're familiar with such matters. In military terms when you have people coming from Livno and Duvno, from Western Herzegovina to bring the strength of the units up, well, what was the purpose, in military terms, of -- of these enforcements? Were they there to reinforce the units? Was something being prepared? What was the military objective in your opinion, on your side? How was this reinforcement perceived? Perhaps a different sort of question will be pursued later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the HVO's pretext was they were preparing for an attack on Kupres in Gornji Vakuf. We knew or, rather, I assumed and was convinced that the HVO was massing its forces there to attack and take Gornji Vakuf after this had been done in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the 3rd Corps commander, General Hadzihasanovic, had they been informed of these important reinforcements that you had noticed? Mr. Mundis' question was what steps did you take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We informed the 3rd Corps about all changes in the situation in a timely fashion. General Hadzihasanovic ordered us to monitor the situation but not to take any military action. We knew that if the HVO wanted to attack Kupres from the direction of Radusa, from the direction of Skrte. They wouldn't be able to do this without us being aware of the fact. We had a battalion there, at the line facing Kupres. So the pretext they gave massing forces in the town was that they would attack Kupres, but this was quite an academic pretext.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, again, sir, following what you've told us was this build-up and what was your assumption concerning what the HVO was doing, did you protest to General Hadzihasanovic that additional steps needed to be taken?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Well, you can't protest in the army, but we requested that he take certain measures at his level to ensure that no other clashes or conflicts broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you recall, sir, whether there were any meetings in November and December, 1992, between the ARBiH and the HVO concerning attempts to stabilise the situation in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: No, there weren't any official meetings during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification to the earlier question. He said that he did make some requests. Was this to General Hadzihasanovic? To whom did he make the request? As I understand it, his superiors were in -- somewhere else. In Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is a question I wanted to put to you since -- but since I know that we're short of time, all of us, I didn't put the question. But since the Defence is asking for this: When you saw that the HVO was obtaining reinforcements, did you send any reports or messages to General Hadzihasanovic to inform him of the situation and to suggest, perhaps, that certain measures should be taken? So did you send any reports, are there any traces of these reports, and did General Hadzihasanovic issue any orders to you and any precise orders with regard to the problem? Did he issue any orders for you to deal with the HVO amassing forces there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is something we were involved in at the beginning of the November. At the time an order had been issued to calm the situation down, and we were trying to find a way of doing this, of calming down the situation. A group of officers arrived in Gornji Vakuf, a group of officers from the HVO and the ABiH, and their objective was to take control of the situation the following way: In their assessment, the armija and HVO were on good terms in Mostar and General Milivoj Petkovic and Arif Pasalic had agreed on sending in a team to make an assessment, and an officer was to be sent to the HVO command in Gornji Vakuf. And from my command -- and to my command a -- an army member from the 4th Corps was supposed to come. This was done. But this form of cooperation didn't last for long, and seven days later everyone had been called back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You haven't answered the question. What we would like to know is whether there were any written reports on the situation, reports from the 317th Mountain Brigade to the 3rd Corps, and did the 3rd Corps respond to such reports? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a misunderstanding. It was the brigade's duty to send an operative report every day, in the morning and in the evening. And this problem was emphasised in each report, and we asked for instructions as to how to act. The corps commander stated quite explicitly that the situation had to be put under control and that we should not allow an armed conflict to break out whatever the cost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Brigadier Agic, did there come a time when the issue of liaison officers was discussed as a means of reducing tension between the ARBiH and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Yes, and agreement was reached at this meeting about this, that liaison officers from the 4th Corps and from the HVO in Mostar did come to the command of the 317th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, when you talk about this meeting, you say agreement was reached at this meeting. When was this meeting and where was this meeting?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I think it was held at the beginning of November in the brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who attended -- who attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: General Pasalic, Zejnil Delalic. I think Vehbija Karic. And on behalf of the HVO General Praljak and some officers that I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, what General Praljak was wearing when he attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: No. This was a higher-level meeting that I did not attend. It was dusk. I don't remember too well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just so we're clear then. At this meeting you were not in attendance?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any other meetings that General Praljak attended?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of August I met General Praljak when with Mr. Musa Fikret he held a meeting in the Radusa hotel, in the banquet room. That is when we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there any other occasions when you met General Praljak or were in attendance at meetings where he was present at?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: No. Perhaps on the Motorola we may have communicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's continue, then, sir, with the period moving into early January, 1993. What was the state of relations between the ARBiH and the HVO in that period of time, the beginning of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: When the new year came there was a lot of uncertainty. It was an ugly period for Central Bosnia. Jajce was captured. There were a lot of refugees, and there was a problem of humanitarian convoys that were being looted and stopped. It was a very difficult situation, generally speaking, for the whole territory. But I must say that the HVO continued to reinforce its forces in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Before we turn to town, I'd like to ask you if you could expand upon the answer where you indicated there was a problem of humanitarian convoys that were being looted and stopped. What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: In those days, and I'm talking about the beginning of 1993, there wasn't a single convoy that was safe unless it was escorted by UNPROFOR. Communications were halted by the HVO for men who had come from Western Europe to spend the holidays at home. As they went back, their passports were seized and they couldn't go back to work in Germany, Austria, Switzerland, and so on. This complicated the situation. We intervened, but I have to point out that even until then no Bosniak could leave Vakuf and go to Prozor without showing an HVO certificate saying that he had paid a hundred Deutschmarks for passage. And this was operational throughout 1992 and the beginning of 1993. They charged the sum in the municipality, that is the HVO, one hundred German marks for each person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Witness, Brigadier, I would like to ask you about the following: It is a follow-up question which was previously asked of you, but somehow I fear that you were not able to answer with certainty. It was asked, had you met General Praljak later on, apart from the one meeting which you mentioned, and you said that, "No, apart from the Motorola incident." Now, I would like to refer to your statement which was distributed, and page 5 of the statement, the very last paragraph mentioning the following that -- in the very last three lines, actually: "In December 1992, Praljak, wearing an HV uniform came to my office with Jasmin Jaganjac, a Croatian army officer, Arif Pasalic, and Zejnil Delalic, both from the Bosnian army. They dispatched a liaison officer to my army and a Croatian officer to the HVO," et cetera. So I would like to clarify this situation in -- concerning your previous statement. Was it a meeting proper or was it only a passing meeting with General Praljak when you refer to the fact that he actually was wearing HV -- HV uniform? So it is my question, if you would be able to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said this in 2000, and when we wanted to change it yesterday, we didn't. But I remember General Praljak very well. I saw him that evening. I didn't attend the meeting because I'm a soldier. I don't ask why. We said hello in passing, and we were sitting in my office because it was the most suitable place for the people to hold their meeting there.
