And I believe that this commission was at the level of a state commission, as General Pasalic had authority from the Supreme Command Staff to discuss matters on behalf of the army and regulate things on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you don't remember how he was clothed, what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General -- General Praljak had a green uniform. Over his jacket he had a belt with a pistol. For a general, rather a large pistol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But you don't remember whether he had an insignia, a particular badge? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he did have insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you don't remember with precision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps -- perhaps we could have a further clarification of something the witness said at page 46, lines 17 and 18 where he said, "When we wanted to change it yesterday, we didn't. I said this in 2000, and when we wanted to change it yesterday, we didn't." That was in response to Judge Prandler's question, but in fact at that passage that is His Honour referred to at the bottom of page 5, there is a certain change that has been made. I wonder whether the Judge might appreciate a further clarification of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When you met with the Prosecutor yesterday, he must have read to you word by word your written statement. You didn't consider it useful at that point to make any corrections. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. Let me explain. When you look at the changes that I made together with the Prosecutor yesterday, these were all grammatical errors and errors in the translation. There were no substantive changes with respect to my statement of 2000. When we discussed this particular passage yesterday, how I saw General Praljak, the Prosecutor wouldn't somehow let me make the changes as it would change my statement, and that is the explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you made changes of grammatical nature. "They appointed a liaison officer," and this is replaced by "They wanted to appoint a liaison officer."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There were some clumsy translations and words that simply don't fit into the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier Agic, can we return to the issue of early January, 1993, and the state of the relationship between the ARBiH and the HVO in Gornji Vakuf in early January, 1993. Can you explain that to us, please?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Prohibition on the return of people to Western Germany for employment caused a lot of problems for all of us. People were afraid to lose their jobs, and in most cases these were people who had spent years working in the Federal Republic of Germany, Switzerland, and Sweden for several years before the war already. Throughout Europe, in fact. The arrival of units that were not from the area in such a highly tense situation is extremely dangerous. However, this was not concealed. Reinforcements were brought in even after the new year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many reinforcements, to the best of your knowledge and information that you received, were brought in after the new year 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I think that until the 10th of January in 1993 about -- between 500, 600 men were brought in, which would be the strength of a battalion, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, sir, were these men brought in by the HVO or by the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: The HVO. They joined their forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us about the rough numbers of men within the 317th Mountain Brigade and the Gornji Vakuf TO Staff in the period late October, 1992, until early January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: At positions facing Kupres, we held forces of battalion and a half strength. Between 700 and 800 men were there. Part of those battalions -- or, rather, the rest of the battalion was in reserve. So would had the following way of working on the lines: One-third on the lines out of the total manpower, one-third in reserve, and one-third at home resting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you, sir, at any point between late October, 1992, and early January, 1993, make requests for additional men from the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: At the time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: It was not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: It wasn't necessary because General Hadzihasanovic, by his orders had expressly prohibited even internal transfers of manpower within our zone of responsibility in Gornji Vakuf, and each of us received specific orders prohibiting this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are throwing us into some perplexion. You just explained that a third were on the lines, a third in reserve, and a third at home resting. That was the situation with respect to the BiH. On the other hand we have 700 HVO who are not at home nor in reserve. That is a force that is present there. So there's something that in military terms seems to have been the result of the arrival of 500 men. You have told us that Hadzihasanovic prohibited the movement of any men, so the 3rd Corps didn't require any particular attention. Is that how you saw the arrival of these 500 men on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We told General Hadzihasanovic every time in our reports about this. And in the second half of December, he was in Zenica, in the 3rd Corps Command, and he -- he repeated that we mustn't allow a conflict with the HVO under any circumstances for the simple reason that whatever entered Bosnia-Herzegovina in those days came through Gornji Vakuf. It was the closest route to Central Bosnia. And should there be a conflict in Gornji Vakuf this would be blocked, and this would cause difficulties for the whole region to the north of Gornji Vakuf. And as a military man, I could understand that, and I knew why the conflict had to be avoided at all cost. And General Hadzihasanovic was aware of this fact, and he understood my fear. And I could feel angry, but I couldn't show my anger against the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that you were not on the same wavelength as General Hadzihasanovic. So 500 people arrived and for a while nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Brigadier Agic, at this point in time, that is early January 1993, were you aware of political developments at the international level to bring about peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Partially, yes. Actually, I knew quite well what was going on, but the population did not. Gornji Vakuf was far away from the world in those days. There were no TV broadcasts, or, rather, those who followed the TV from Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was interrupted at the beginning of 1992. So we couldn't watch the news. The press didn't reach Gornji Vakuf. Some of the command officers were aware of this through the information service of the 3rd Corps that negotiations were under preparation in Geneva, and I could -- frequently spoke to military observers who would drop by and would leave papers that they had. When they came from Zagreb they would bring the newspapers so that I knew what was under preparation with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I think that the international factors were absolutely opposed to any conflict between the Bosniaks and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you were referring to the negotiations under preparation in Geneva, what specifically were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Plan, about the formation of provinces in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, earlier this afternoon as reflected on page 30, lines 20 and 21 of the transcript, you said in the evening of the 20th and 21st of October there was an exchange of fire in the town and the HVO fired several projectiles on the town. Was that an isolated incident or was more of that to come?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: It was an isolated incident. There was an exchange of fire in town, and I said we managed to calm things down by the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's focus now, sir, on January, 1993. Did the situation in Gornji Vakuf remain peaceful throughout the month of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: January? In January?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: It was peaceful until the 10th or 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened on the 10th or 11th of January, 1993, in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: On that day, I found time to take my two sons into town. At between 1707 and 1710, two mortar shells of 82 millimetres were fired from the direction of Mackovac, and they fell at the entrance of the town near the bridge close to the fire brigade centre at a distance of 10 to 15 metres between the two. I took -- I returned the children to my wife immediately and went to the brigade headquarters. I was told about these two projectiles. I said that I had heard it, I almost saw it, and I asked what had -- what it was all about. I called UNPROFOR, and they arranged a meeting, and Mr. Tokic Zrinko and myself came. The response was that two irresponsible, drunken soldiers had fired those two shells. After that, the police exchanged fire in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, sir. When you say "after that," how long after these two shells was this exchange of fire between the police? The same day, the next day, a week later? Can you give us an idea of the time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: That same day, between an hour and 40 minutes or two hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say that UNPROFOR arranged a meeting between Mr. Tokic and yourself, how was this meeting conducted?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: It was an ordinary working meeting. I asked what was going on, and he admitted that this was due to lack of discipline and that two soldiers in a drunken state had fired those two shells. And I said, "Why do you need mortars in that region, because this is a region that can only hit Gornji Vakuf or -- within a circle of 360 degrees and within the range of an 82-millimetre mortar?" He wasn't ready for this query on my part, but I understood clearly why they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At that point in time, sir, January 10th or 11th, 1993, how far were the VRS lines from the town of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I don't want to be mistaken, but I'd say it was between 15 and 20 kilometres as the crow flies, maybe even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And this meeting that you had with Zrinko Tokic following these two mortar shells landing in the town, where was it held?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: At UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where was UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was right next to the HVO headquarters in the ball bearings factory and the factory Yassa, and the ball bearings factories are one next to the other. They share a common fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When was the next time after this meeting with Zrinko Tokic that you were at the UNPROFOR building next to the HVO headquarters?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: We met again on the 12th in the afternoon, but this was preceded by a virtually day-long shooting in town, and occasionally even artillery weapons were being used. So the town had become a target. But it was my assessment that it was by mistake that someone had started the attack early, that the forces were not ready for the attack. And this was something that in a sense saved Gornji Vakuf from the destiny suffered by Prozor. Time will show whether I'm right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you elaborate upon what you mean by it was a mistake that someone had started the attack early?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would ask also, it assumes an attack was planned. It begs the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you will have plenty of time during the cross-examination. I don't know what you wanted to say, but generally you have just said many things. You discover that there were two shells of 82 millimetres that fell. The official version of the HVO is that two drunken soldiers -- let's say that's possible in any unit; occasionally this type of incident may occur. But then you added there was an exchange of fire with the police. We don't know whether it was the HVO police who fired at the BH or vice versa. You didn't explain that. And then listening to you, you're explaining that in the afternoon there were exchanges. We, the Judges, would like to know who was the aggressor. Was it, as you seem to imply, an attempt at an attack which was aborted because they weren't ready, or was it an isolated incident? What counts for us is your analysis of this event. To save time, could you tell us exactly what your understanding of it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an undisputed fact that two mortar shells were fired. I can understand the possibility of two soldiers getting drunk. All armies in the world drink, and so did ours. What I can't understand is why this 82-millimetre mortar was positioned in the spot from where the fire came. This is what is unacceptable militarily in this case, because enemy lines are nowhere near that position. Furthermore, there was an exchange of fire between the HVO police and the 317th Brigade in the centre of town, next to the main shop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we learned that there was an exchange of fire between the HVO police and your own soldiers. So who was the first to shoot, yours or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please carry on. So the HVO can fire. So what did this mean in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it meant that the plan to take Gornji Vakuf was being implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you immediately contact the 3rd Corps to inform them of the fact that certain events were unfolding in the field? Did you inform them of the fact immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I immediately informed the 3rd Corps Command of the fact, and I reported to them on the situation in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I note that the witness has been provided with two bundles of documents. I ask at this point that he be shown -- or that the witness take the bundle and look at document numbered 643.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Brigadier Agic, just for the record, you were shown both of these bundles of documents yesterday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you actually took those bundles with you to your hotel last night and reviewed all of these documents. Is that -- is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, document 643, when was the first time you ever saw this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment on the contents of this document P 643?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Well, this relates to the question that you put to me when you asked me what the situation was like in October and November. I said that the tension was constant, that contact was poor, that it was difficult to move around, to establish communications, that it was difficult to use the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How does this document relate to these issues that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that it was difficult to move around the area. It was difficult to use the roads. You couldn't do anything without HVO escort in the areas that were under their control. You had to announce your intention to go somewhere and then you would be accompanied by HVO police, and this included everyone. This included the Merhamet organisation too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to turn to document number 712. Again, when was the first time you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment on this document and its contents with respect to the events in Gornji Vakuf municipality?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: It's not true that it was on the 23rd of October that -- it's not true that we were amassing forces. This is correct. I said that on the 23rd we were attempting to make sure that the situation in Prozor didn't have repercussions in Gornji Vakuf. We were trying to ensure that the conflict didn't escalate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see, sir, the reference to 24 October, where the document indicates all BH Army units were ordered to full combat readiness at 0500 hours? Can you comment on that aspect of this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: You're referring to the 24th?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes and again this report has two reports one on Gornji Vakuf and one on Prozor and I'd ask you to make sure you're looking at the Gornji Vakuf part of the report.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: The 22nd, in Voljevac two buses arrived. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Make sure do you have number 712?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could go to the third page in the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I haven't got three pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could see, sir, the entry under the 24th of October.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I can see that. This isn't true. We didn't order full combat readiness for the units because we were working all day on the 23rd to put things under control, to put an end to the conflict. The exchange of fire between ABiH members and the HVO. Not a single unit had been ordered to take up a position outside the town. It's true that on the 24th of October in the village of Voljevac as it's stated in this HVO police report, it's true that two buses arrived in the Voljevac sector with ABiH members, but we would operate in that area. And these people didn't have the right to go back through Prozor because of the situation in Prozor and Novi Travnik. At my request, when I requested this from the commander in Prozor, I knew him personally. I couldn't get to him that evening, so as a result we decided to send the unit back and they were sent back to Konjic, and from Konjic via Parsovic [phoen] they arrived in the village around Voljevac. They arrived in the Voljevac sector and they remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Brigadier Agic if you could now turn to document 1087. Again, sir, when was the first time you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment on this document and particularly the reference to Geneva?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: What I'm certain of -- or, rather, I became certain of the fact last night is that my claim with regard to the HVO attack on Gornji Vakuf is correct. This was an attack that had been prepared, and I became certain of this last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you now turn, sir, to document 1107. And again, my preliminary question is when was the first time you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask you to draw your attention, sir, to the first paragraph of this document, and I'd like to ask you to comment on what's contained in that first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I said a while ago with regard to individuals who were being arrested and with regard to movement, I said that that was a problem. I can't remember that in the part of town under the control of the armija, I can't remember there being a Croatian flag. But in the introduction it says that the civilian authorities were not functioning, and someone felt that as a result, since the civilian authorities were not functioning an order could be issued, an attempt could be made to take the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in this document, in the first paragraph I can see that ABiH forces arrived from Central Bosnia. They arrived in Gornji Vakuf. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During this period when this order was issued, I claim with full responsibility that there was not a single soldier in the area of Gornji Vakuf on the 12th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what this states does not reflect the truth as you experienced the events at the time it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, what about the statement, "... the BH army is attempting to take over certain key buildings in Gornji Vakuf ..."? The first -- in the first part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Well, there were no any -- there were no longer any key facilities. The HVO had control of all the key facilities in and around the town. So all the facilities in and around Vakuf were under HVO control and at the border they even had a centre for interception. It was in the Rog centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about the last paragraph the attempt by the BH army to eliminate the HVO in Gornji Vakuf? Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I can't because this seems illogical to me. I don't know what it is that we did to try to eliminate the HVO. Perhaps we wanted to persuade them somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you look, sir, under the heading "Order", the first paragraph or number 1 under order, towards the end of number 1 there's reference to "... prevent the enemy from threatening the Croatian population in Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf." Can you comment on that? Threats to the Croat population in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what they should be protected from in this area under the control of the armija. In that area there were certain Croats, not many of them. They had received flats as a result of the positions they occupied, as a result of their jobs. But given the area under the armija control, well, there was just one old family, the Kovacevic family, and in that area there wasn't a single house inhabited by a Croat. After the Second World War, none such houses had been built. Only Bosniaks had houses there. Only the old Kovacevic family had a house there, and that's still the case today. So I really don't see how someone's property might have been at risk or anything else for that matter. And I won't comment on the situation in Bugojno. Item 1 of the order says, "Break up the enemy forces of the ABiH in Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, based on what's contained in paragraph -- or number 6 of this document, can you as a professional soldier characterise this order?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, these things took place on a daily basis. Forces would take people in incessantly. As far as item 5 is concerned, I interpret it as follows: Some of the HVO forces were sent to Bugojno in order to divide or to cut off Gornji Vakuf from the direction of Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What does 6 mean in military terms? What does 6 mean, where it says, "Combat. Be prepared for combat activity immediately."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this an order. It says be prepared for combat activity immediately. Well, that is order. I don't understand why it "says to be started when I gave the order." If you have such an order, that's sufficient. You have to be ready for combat activity. It's sufficient to implement this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But couldn't we interpret this as order that says there will be an action, but I'll say when this should be started? In English it says, "when I give the order."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what it says in my document too. I think that these two shells were fired from 82-millimetre mortars, and as a result this plan had been disturbed. Otherwise, things wouldn't have unfolded in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier Agic, at this point in time, that is mid-January, 1993, to whom were you reporting?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I reported to the 3rd Corps. Unfortunately, the time the corps was the immediate superior command of the brigades. So the brigade commander and the staff would always send extraordinary reports with regard to every event. The 3rd Corps commander was well-informed of this situation. I then requested that officers from the Corps Command should be sent to help us deal with this situation, because these were matters that were beyond our authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, how did you submit reports to the 3rd Corps? By what means did you submit reports to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: All the brigades had so-called switch communications. This was a means whereby one would send reports or any other documents. You'd use a modem to send such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, that was just translated, at least into English, as "switch communications." Was this also known as Paket communications?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We call this form of communication Paket communications. I'm not an expert in this field so I wouldn't go into the details. I wouldn't want to explain how this actually functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How frequently would you produce these reports to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: As I have already said we had to send such reports twice a day but, given the situation, whenever there was an incident, an event of any importance, we would react immediately and send reports to the Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd asks you now, Brigadier Agic, to turn to number 1132?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, before we get to this particular document which is dated 14 January, since the gentleman indicated that he was sending reports twice a day, and on special incidents he would also send one, perhaps the gentleman could tell it us, where are the other documents, the documents that he was generating on the 11th, the 12th, the 13th, the twice a day, plus the extra ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 11th, 12th, and 13th of January you sent reports to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These reports must have been filed or registered in a logbook. They must have been given certain numbers. There must be a written trace of the reports that you sent to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a response from the corps commander in front of me, a response to our requests. This is what the Prosecution was referring to, 1132.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that's a different document. We'll see about that later. But on the 11th, 12th, and 13th, you're saying that you sent reports to the 3rd Corps, reports on the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, even before. We'd send reports in the morning and in the evening. It was our duty to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite clear about this, because I have time limitations that have to be respected and to avoid questions -- to avoid putting questions to you that aren't very helpful, my question is very simple. Before the 18th of January, 1993, are you saying that you never received an order to attack the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, document 1132, when was the first time you ever saw this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Last night was the first time I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment on what's contained in this document? First of all, why don't you tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: The corps commander requested in this document that the Chief of Staffs of the armed forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina should be made familiar with the situation of the -- in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. In fact, he informed them of the situation. He informed these commanders of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the references in here, sir, to Gornji Vakuf, if you could focus your attention on those. There are a few places where Gornji Vakuf is mentioned, particularly in the middle of the document. Do you see those references?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I can't see it very well, but I can make out the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the middle of the page there is a paragraph which relates directly to what you said about the 500 individuals who arrived. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: No. I can see a paragraph where it mentions 500 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't read it, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In fact, the copy is not very good. Mr. Mundis, I'm looking at the B/C/S version of the document, and it's very difficult to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It is. It is indeed, Mr. President. I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, the simplest thing to do would be for you to read out the paragraph and ask what the witness thinks about it. The interpreters can then interpret it into the witness's language, and it will be just as if he read it himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me just -- so that there's no confusion, in the middle of page 2, in the English translation it says as follows: "Accordingly, around 500 such HVO members were deployed in the previous 10 days in the wider area of Novi Travnik, Gornji Vakuf, and along the Gornji Vakuf-Bugojno stretch. Upon this, there occurred an open artillery attack, followed by an infantry attack on Gornji Vakuf." Does this report and analysis submitted by General Hadzihasanovic up the chain of command to the RBiH Armed Forces Command Staff accurately reflect the situation in the middle of January, 1993, with respect to Gornji Vakuf and the immediate area?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: In does reflect the situation, but I don't think the position of the artillery was correctly noted. The artillery can't act in Gornji Vakuf if it has this calibre. It was positioned between Pidris and Mackovac, on the left side in the Dobrasin sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, where -- where are you seeing that in this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Well, it says from the firing positions, Pajic Polje and the village of Rumboci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's the paragraph immediately below the one that I just read out to you, but I was concerned about what's contained in the paragraph preceding that.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: On the 14th the HVO carried out infantry attacks, and they tried to attain their objective in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you report that information to General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: And on the 13th, he promised that a team of officers would be September to Gornji Vakuf to assist in the negotiations and to halt what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. This might be an appropriate spot for the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And before we take a break, Mr. President, just a correction on the transcript. I believe it was page 65, line 21. The witness said that it "was not correctly noted." As it reflects now, it says "was correctly noted." So I think that needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My understanding was that in this report by General Hadzihasanovic to the Supreme Command he positioned the HVO artillery in two positions, Pajic Polje and the village of Rumboci, and you said that there must be an error because they weren't there. They were somewhere else. Is that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It says Rumboci correctly, but the artillery wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the benefit of the transcript, the artillery, according to you, was situated where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The artillery was between the village of Pidris and Mackovci [phoen]. I apologise. I am not counting 82-millimetre mortars as artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when you're talking about artillery, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to calibres of a hundred and more millimetres, guns and howitzers. The 130-millimetre gun and so on. 82 millimetres is an infantry weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And would you include tanks in this group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tanks are armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is half past 5.00. We will have a 20-minute break, and we will resume work after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, we have an hour and 10 minutes at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Brigadier Agic, I'd now ask you to turn to document -- let me ask you a couple of questions before we get to the next document. Middle of January 1993, can -- were you aware, based on the position that you held, as to events occurring in the villages in Gornji Vakuf municipality outside the town of Gornji Vakuf itself?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: We were more or less familiar with the situation in all the villages, wherever we had units of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How were you familiar? Was it based on reports you received or speaking to people? How did you receive this information as to what was going on in the area around the town of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: First of all, by means of communications with subordinate units. We had to contact and coordination with them. Then also upon the initiative of the UNPROFOR commander in Gornji Vakuf it was agreed that I and Mr. Tokic Zrinko in the evening of the 13th of January, 1993, should tour the lower part of Gornji Vakuf municipality, which meant we would tour Duratbegovic Dolac, Draza Dolac, Pajic Polje, Hrasnica, and Grnica, and that is what we did. In all these localities we spoke to the unit commanders, but I must point out that in Pajic Polje I was not allowed to leave the transporter because Mr. Zrinko Tokic could not guarantee my security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask you now sir to take a look at document 1126. When was the first time you saw this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I saw this document last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment on what's contained in this document in terms of the accuracy of the information?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I can comment on the part referring to Gornji Vakuf. Voljevac and Pridvorci were shot at with multiple-rocket launchers, and the other place with artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how did you come to know that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: From the report of the 2nd Battalion commander in Donji Boljevci. He was precise, asking what he should do, and it's not far away because you can hear the sound of such weapons. And in town we felt it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier Agic, can you tell us what was occurring in the town of Gornji Vakuf on the 14th and 15th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: In the afternoon of the 14th, I think it was about 3.00 p.m., three persons came from Zenica. That is, a delegation of the armed forces from Bosnia-Herzegovina with the addition of a representative of the ruling circles of the SDA. I think the gentleman was a member of the SDA, and he was a representative in the parliament of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Dzemal Merdan came, deputy commander of the 3rd Corps; Selmo Cikotic, member of the Corps Command; and Salcinovic, I cannot recall his first name, who was a deputy in the republic's parliament and the most responsible person of the SDA in the then ruling structure in Zenica. On behalf of the HVO the meeting was attended by Colonel Andric and Colonel Zeljko Siljeg. And there was another member and I cannot recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, first of all, what the purpose of this meeting was?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: The purpose was to put a stop to combat operations and to come to an agreement how to restore the situation to the previous situation in -- to the previous condition in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did anything occur at this meeting that stuck out in your mind?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: At this meeting Colonel Andric produced a document of the government of Herceg-Bosna, of the republic of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, which specifies that the forces of the army in Gornji Vakuf must immediately be placed under the command of the HVO. And a second document described how to implement that decision, and the third, what the consequences would be if that were not to be carried out. And it was signed by the Prime Minister of the government of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you actually see this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I did. Yes, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did the meeting develop after this letter was produced or this document was produced by Colonel Andric?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: It was a very awkward situation for all those present, especially for those on my side of the table. I even felt that representatives of the international community were astonished. Colonel Stewart was present, BritBat commander from Vitez. I think his name was Raymond Lee, the head of the observers based in Zenica. We were all astonished. And when Mr. Andric asked the others to comment, Dzemal Merdan said that this was beyond his powers as president of this commission and that he would have to return to Zenica to consult with the corps commander. At the end, Colonel Siljeg commented where he took this decision of the government of Herceg-Bosna, that this would be done willy-nilly, that it would be carried out. It was an ultimatum. And then representatives of the international community asked for time for the delegation of the BH army to consult with higher-level authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Once this document was produced and these comments that you've told us about were made, how much longer did the meeting continue?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: There was a break, as far as I can remember, for people to take some coffee and to discuss amongst themselves, and this lasted perhaps a little longer than half an hour. And when it was resumed, it didn't take long. I think it ended about 17.45. Dzemal Merdan asked to return to Zenica together with this gentleman from the SDA. I've just forgotten his name. However, they couldn't receive guarantees for safe return, and they were taken to Zenica in the warriors of the British Battalion, and Colonel Stewart gave them these vehicles to go back to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, a few moments ago, as reflected on page 69, lines 24 and 25, you indicated that this document, the third part of this document contained what the consequences would be if that were not to be carried out. Do you remember what these consequences were as set forth in this document that you saw?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: In item 3, it was stated, to paraphrase, that the HVO would disarm such units by force and place them under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask you now, sir, if you would turn your attention to document 1131. When was the first time, sir, that you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like you to look, if you would, on the Bosnian language version of this document towards the bottom where there's reference to a state commission of the BH army arriving at around 1600 hours. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: That is the commission, and it was about 1500 hours, not 1600.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you read that portion of the document, please? And then I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about what's contained on that section.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Does this document reflect what occurred at the meeting that took place on the 14th of January, 1993, that you attended?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: It does. Agreement was reached that a delegation of the army would return to Zenica and consult with their superiors, and that efforts would be made to halt combat operations until an official position is obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, General -- Brigadier: The document, does it make reference to this, as you've described it, ultimatum that was produced by Colonel Andric?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: It doesn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see in the -- in the bullet point immediately below Mr. Salcinovic's name reference to a statement? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to be asking counsel to be very careful not to lead the witness because the witness indicated that it was a decision and then counsel later on referred to it as a letter. I didn't object then but at this point I would just kindly ask that we proceed with a great deal of caution, because the decision has been introduced and we will be looking at it, I take it, at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I take Counsel Karnavas's point. This document refers to a statement, and that's what I'm asking the witness about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see the reference in this document to the statement?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this is an HVO report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment on the sentence that says: "The commission consisting of the said members entirely supports and accepts the statement"? Do you know, sir, what this is referring to based on your attendance at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: It was officially agreed, and when they say statement, representatives of the media were present, and it was officially announced that the commission would adjourn until higher-level authorities are consulted with a view to overcoming the newly created situation. And probably the reference here is to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, to the best of your recollection how long did Dzemal Merdan remain in town after this meeting was completed?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Dzemal Merdan, in a UN Warrior, came to town, came to my office. He wrote a telegram for General Hadzihasanovic, and within half an hour he left Gornji Vakuf to go to Zenica with Mr. Salcinovic. Merdan suggested, and General Hadzihasanovic accepted, that Selmo Cikotic, as a member of this commission and a member of the Corps Command, should remain in Gornji Vakuf and should try with HVO representatives to keep the situation under control as much as possible until further decisions were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recall -- Brigadier Agic, do you recall how long Mr. Cikotic remained in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cikotic left Vakuf, I think, on the 17th or 18th. He went to Zenica for consultations and then he returned the next day. He remained in Gornji Vakuf until the truce was signed on behalf of the HVO by General Milivoj Petkovic and, on behalf of the army, General Arif Pasalic. And he stayed until that day in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that -- that Dzemal Merdan was going to take this ultimatum, as you've described it, to higher authorities because it wasn't something that he was able to deal with at his level. Did he ever come back to you or to the other people who were participating with a response?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Dzemal Merdan did not come back, and he couldn't interpret the first item because there was mention made of the Vance-Owen Plan and the cantons with the Bosniak or Croat majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask you, sir, to take a look at the document marked 1174. When was the first time, Brigadier Agic, that you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I saw it last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, can you comment on what this document is in terms of who produced and when and where, if you know?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I think that this document was compiled in the 3rd Corps on the basis of a report by Mr. Merdan from these negotiations which were conducted early on and the report which a member of the corps, Mr. Cikotic, would send to the 3rd Corps Command on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what might seem to be a discrepancy that the document indicates Gornji Vakuf, 16/1/1993 at 1845 hours? This is on the top of the document in your language in the middle of the first page on the left-hand side. Was General Merdan in Gornji Vakuf on that day, at that time, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: No, Dzemal Merdan was not in Gornji Vakuf on that day. Mr. Cikotic spent the whole day on behalf of the army in the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And now, sir, if you can see towards, again in the Bosnian language, at the bottom of the first page and the top of the second page, there are a number of bullet points. Were you aware of what's contained in these bullet points on this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's turn to document 1146. Before we do that, though, let me ask you this question: There appears to be a reference to you in this document. Again, in one of the bullet points.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I am mentioned in the second bullet point, that there's a request that command of the army can no longer be carried out through Topcic, Agic, and Prijic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any point in time, sir, were you familiar or were you aware that this demand was being made?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I was, because earlier on, on the 12th, when we were talking, that is something that they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say on the 12th, what are you -- what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: When I said that we had meetings with UNPROFOR daily and we were endeavouring to come to an agreement with the assistance of UNPROFOR and representatives of the staffs and HVO brigades from Bugojno joined in. And these mixed teams, efforts were made for a member of the Bosnian units to go to HVO commands, that a Bosniak from the 307th Brigade should go to the HVO, such attempts were made. And I can't remember the name of -- the HVO representative from the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade in Bugojno came to our command, but there were problems on the ground. We withdrew a person who was at Pidris, at the command post at Pidris on behalf of the army. So these attempts were being made constantly to stop the conflict, because losses were considerable, casualties were high, destruction enormous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, sir, to please look at document 1146. I would like to be absolutely clear, Brigadier Agic, is this decision that you have before you the document that you saw, that was presented by Colonel Andric at the meeting on the 14th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Well, the important difference is the following: There was no signature because it was sent by Paket communications. I believe they used a similar system in the HVO. It didn't have this number of items and I believe it was a document that concerned the municipality of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So is the answer no?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Is that -- is that the decision you saw or not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's not this decision. The decision I saw was that Colonel Andric had three items. It hadn't been signed. It had arrived via Paket communications, and it had been placed on our desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I don't believe this decision could have been shown to the witness, the date of the 15th of January. So it couldn't have been shown on the 14th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just for a further point of clarification or confusion, whichever may be the case, if we go back to document 1174 where the gentleman said that he hadn't seen this document, if you look at -- under paragraph 2, the first bulletin point, it says the HVO decision on the organisation of provinces is a temporary decision based on reciprocity. And then it talks -- the next one talks about the Geneva agreement. So I would suspect that there's going to be some clarification whether the gentleman perhaps might be just simply confused with the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you spoke about a document that had three items in it. The first one concerned the fact that the ABiH forces had to be under the -- placed under the HVO, and then we had implementation and three consequences. Then you said that this document, as far as you can remember, had been sent -- had been signed by Prlic. Here we have a document as the Defence has rightly pointed out, and the date is the 15th of January, the date of the document. So this can't be the document in question. The document that you saw on the 14th that had been signed by Prlic, are you quite certain that you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have said, I haven't seen this document. I saw a different document. It had three items, and I said that it didn't bear a signature. And we were told that it had been sent via Paket communications. You can't sign documents that are sent by this -- by this way -- in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But was the name Prlic at the bottom of the document, although it hadn't been signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And the Defence also asked me something else. These are the items, as I have said, but General Hadzihasanovic says that there were requests made at the meeting that had to be complied with. There was the HVO decision on structuring units and, on the basis of reciprocity, the HVO wanted this to be done at this meeting. They asked for units to be withdrawn in the direction of the villages. All units in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf that weren't from Gornji Vakuf should be withdrawn from Gornji Vakuf. The HVO said they wouldn't shell, and then there were other requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the decision of the 15th of January, 1146, you'd never seen it before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me go back to document 1174, if you still have that before you, 1174.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on the text of the second paragraph, it would appear that there was a meeting at 1730 hours on the 16th of January, 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I said that Mr. Cikotic stayed on in town, and every day he had meetings with some HVO officers, and they tried to reach an agreement so an end could be put to the conflict. I think this is based on his report. Mr. Tokic Zrinko and myself were only called upon if it was necessary to do something concrete and if it was necessary to convey orders to us and inform us of what had been agreed upon in UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recall, Brigadier Agic, at how many meetings of these you were called in, either you or -- yourself and Mr. Tokic, in this period in the middle of January, 1993, while Selmo Cikotic was still in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Well, on average I think we were called to the UNPROFOR premises at least once a day in order to have consultations with the commission that was there. Sometimes it was more frequent. But it was a problem for me to pass through a certain area to reach UNPROFOR. This area was under HVO control, so I had to use UN armoured carriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, and this was brought to my attention and I apologise for the interruption, but on page 69, 20 going on further down, the gentleman said that he saw three documents, one signed by Mr. Prlic on the 14th. And so, as I recall his testimony, he's saying that such documents couldn't be signed because of the way they were being, you know, transmitted. Now, again, perhaps the Court may invite the witness, you know, to answer whether he is simply mistaken, because after all we're talking about a lot of years, or whether he stands firm, in which case we will need to take the necessary actions in impeaching him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the colonel showed you the document that had arrived by Paket communications, the document that hadn't been sign by Prlic but nevertheless bore his name, was this a document with these three items or were there in fact three documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There was just one document. It was a decision and it consisted of three items. I mentioned three items. I didn't mention three documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how I understood your testimony. It was one document that consisted of three items. We're not talking about three documents. Mr. Karnavas, apparently you seem to think that there were three documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may assist because I had brought it up and brought it to Mr. Karnavas's attention. The testimony reads as follows at that reference: "At this meeting Colonel Andric produced a document of the government of Herceg-Bosna of the republic of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna which specifies that the forces of the army in Gornji Vakuf must immediately be placed under the command of the HVO, and a second document described how to implement that decision, and the third what the consequences would be if that were not to be carried out, and it was signed by the Prime Minister of the government of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Prlic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there perhaps an interpretation error when you answered the question you were referring to one single document, not three documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat what I said. There was one document that consisted of three items. The first one was execution, second implementation, and the third consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But does the gentleman still stand by his testimony under oath earlier on when he says that he saw it signed by Dr. Prlic? There lies the conundrum, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you said "signed," in military terms, well, we can have a document that's sent, a document that bears someone's name but that doesn't have a signature. Is that what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said that the document had been transmitted via Paket communications, and this means that it's impossible for such a document to bear a stamp or someone's signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It wasn't a document that had been faxed. It was a document that was sent electronically via Paket communications, so there was no signature. Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume so. I don't know how the communications department in the HVO actually functions. I assume that they used a modem, Paket communications, which is what we in the armija used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To make sure there is no ambiguity remaining, since Defence is focusing on this, the document did bear Prlic's name but not his signature, his handwritten signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how I understood your answer. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like you now to turn to document 1135. When was the first time you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Last night was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask you, sir, if you could please take a look at the first sentence of this document leading up to the "I hereby issue the following order," and if you could comment on that first sentence for us, please.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the order you're presenting this in. You showed me an order from the commander of the Tomislav operative zone. That was Colonel Siljeg. The date was the 12th of January. And in that order it was ordering that the town be attacked, and I assume that his command or, rather, the Main Staff issued such an order -- drafted such an order on the 15th of January. In the introduction it says "because of the open aggression of the Muslim forces -- the open and treacherous aggression by Muslim forces throughout the HZ HB territory," et cetera, but the introduction in his order, in Mr. Siljeg's order, is different. He orders an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, I would ask you, sir, to focus on this paragraph that you've just started reading, and if you could comment on what's contained in this document.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: In the introduction it mentions Croatian houses being set on fire, but up until the 15th of January, not a single Croatian house had been torched. Up until the 15th of January the situation was quite the reverse. Wherever they arrived everything was set fire to. On the 15th of January, the -- Hrasnica had been entirely burnt down. I can claim with full responsibility that no one attacked Croats in Gornji Vakuf and in the territory of the HZ HB. This is what the Main Staff refers to in the introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't wish to interrupt, but there's nothing in this document that refers to Gornji Vakuf, and I understand that the man is fixated with Gornji Vakuf, and that's his testimony, and we'll see whether that evidence bears out. Perhaps Mr. Mundis could clarify to the gentleman, because this is the 15th, and somehow the gentleman is insisting on marching to his own orders, that he's trying to connect the 12th with the 15th. So I would ask that -- I don't want to interrupt, but he -- simply answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 4, page 2 in the English version, it says Vakuf and Prozor. Vakuf is referred to in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He was asked to look at the preamble and the gentleman begins with the 12th. And he has done this -- this is his second time I would just simply ask that the gentleman -- so we can have a clear record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just briefly respond. This is -- I don't even know how many times Mr. Karnavas has asked for clarification which, with all due respect, are matters for him to raise during cross-examination. We would ask that this time be deducted - for all of these questions - from his cross because that's actually what he's trying to do during the direct examination. Number two, as has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll try to move ahead. There is an order and it has a preamble. In the preamble General Petkovic says that Muslim forces had launched an attack and as a result there were scores of dead and wounded. That concerns HVO soldiers. It also says that Croatian houses were burnt, Croats were expelled, et cetera, et cetera. So the question the Judges are requesting themselves is whether this preamble actually reflects the situation on the ground or not. Is it true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The preamble, the part of the preamble that refers to the aggression, to the expulsion, to the torching of houses, this part of the preamble is false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's just clarify this, sir. Are you speaking about what you were familiar with, that is Gornji Vakuf, when you make this statement that this is false?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Yes. As the Defence said, the preamble can be linked up with item 4, can be related to item 4, where forces in Gornji Vakuf are being strengthened. So the conflict is up there, nowhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the preamble says "throughout HZ HB territory." And I don't know why the witness refuses to look at that part. It's not restricted to Gornji Vakuf. And now the gentleman under oath is saying under no -- in no area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you can raise this issue in the course of your cross-examination. The witness is a high-ranking officer, and as a result he should be aware of what he's saying. You quite rightly pointed out that the preamble mentions the entire territory. Can this preamble be linked up to the situation in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, may I respond? May I clarify this matter, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Combat readiness throughout the area under HVO control should be raised, and it says part of the forces at full combat readiness should arrive in Gornji Vakuf. As far as I know on the 15th of January there were no longer any clashes between the armija and the HVO, in no areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you please look at 1139. When was the first time you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Last night was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, turning your attention to the 15th of January, 1993, again there's reference in the preamble to the Geneva agreements. Do you know what that's referring to?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Which page did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the beginning in the preamble.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: No, which document number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: 1139. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, again, sir, with reference to the date, 15 January 1993, do you know what the reference in the first -- in the preamble of this document, with respect to Geneva agreements, is referring to?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: In the preamble they're referring to areas in which there's a Croatian majority and a Bosniak majority, but they were in a bit of a hurry. The Geneva agreement was never signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And my question is: What is the Geneva agreement? What is that referring to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to speculate. I've never read through the Geneva agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Look under, sir, under number 1, references to provinces 3, 8, and 10. Do you know what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think I should raise an objection now. If the witness said he's not familiar with the contents of the agreement, I think it's really useless to ask the witness about the plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General, you said that at the time you weren't familiar with the Vance-Owen Plan, but on the 15th of January, 1993, did you have contact with the HVO, UNPROFOR, your colleagues, the 3rd Corps, Merdan, and others, and in these contexts did you hear about provinces 3, 8, and 10? Were provinces 3, 8, and 10 discussed when you had such contact at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard about them, but I still don't know which territories are concerned when reference is made to provinces 3, 8, and 10. I don't even know which areas provinces 1, 5, and 9 refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you don't know. But you were aware of the fact that negotiations were under way in Geneva, high-level negotiations, the purpose of which was to find a solution for the problems in your country? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, each and every normal citizen discussed this subject because everyone wanted the war to come to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said there was no television in Gornji Vakuf. What about radios? Were radios functioning at the time or not? Could you listen to Radio Zagreb or Radio Sarajevo? No one listened to the radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no electricity for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but radios can also function with batteries.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we knew that they said that Croatian and Bosniak provinces would be established, and each population, each people would have the majority in certain provinces. They didn't speak about the actual territory that would be covered by these provinces though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You haven't answered my question about the radio. I still don't know whether there was anyone who was able to listen to the radio in Gornji Vakuf on the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, believe me, it's very simple to answer that question. On the 15th of January in Vakuf, the ordinary people were just trying to save their lives. No one had Geneva on their minds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, did this order nevertheless reach you? Did it reach members of the ABiH? Because it was addressed to you so that your forces could be in the provinces concerned and that under HVO control. Because if you were familiar with the order at the time, it concerned you in a certain sense, and you could have asked yourself about the significance of provinces 3, 8, and 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We never received this order, and we were in the chain of command that was part of my 3rd Corps. Whatever I received, whatever orders I received, I received from the 3rd Corps. That included the fact -- well, even if army units should have been placed on someone's command, I should have received such an order from the appropriate commander to carry out at that task in order to report the "new commander."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, everyone saw a series of documents a minute ago, and it seems that -- well, it's not that it seems, it's quite certain or almost certain that ABiH units were to be subordinated to the HVO. But at the same time, in certain areas the situation was the reverse. HVO units were going to be subordinated to the ABiH. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the Vance-Owen Plan was never signed. It never entered into force. It was never implemented. But I knew that this was supposed to happen if it had been signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Colonel Andric says you -- told you this is how it's going to happen, as of the 15th of January you will be subordinated to some body, what was your initial reaction? What did you tell him? "This is madness, and I don't understand. I'm going to refer this matter to my superiors"? What did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The deputy commander of the 3rd Corps reacted calmly to this, or pretended to be calm. My reaction was different. I can't say -- put in words what I said he should do with that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, tell us what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really embarrassed to say that, that he can wipe his behind with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I really would like to refrain from questions, too much questions addressed to you from the Bench, but I would like to ask, for me at least, a final question today, and then when we are addressing the issue to whom the -- this letter, actually not the letter but a comment was developed, and here at the very end, in the very end we find on the page 2, in the English version, to be delivered, number 1, South-eastern Herzegovina operative zone, then the number 2, North-western Herzegovina operative zone, then number 3, Central Bosnia operative zone. 1st Mostar Brigade, that's number 4 and 5. Now my question is to you: If it is there mentioned the various regional operative zones, do you believe, do you consider that your own unit, that is the 317th Brigade, was included, in your view, to those operative zones or not? Because then -- otherwise, you should have received it. If you did not receive it, then it could have been considered a technical or any other problem. But do you -- did you consider yourselves at that time if you received this very kind of order as an addressee, or you really would like to tell us now that these addressees which are mentioned here on page 2, that is to be delivered to those operative zones, that it -- it does not relate to your own unit? So I would like to ask you this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 317th Brigade was part of the 3rd Corps. This order was addressed to operative zones, which up until then were part of the Main Staff of the HVO in Grude. Putting units under the command of the HVO in the provinces would need a restructuring at the state level, a reorganisation of the state whether they be regions, provinces, cantons. In this case, provinces were envisaged. This would mean the reorganisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and within that framework of the armed forces. I cannot on my own initiative as a commander of any Tactical Unit execute this order, because somebody from my chain of command has to give me such an order. We know that the Vance-Owen Plan was not signed, and this order could perhaps have waited until the end of February when it might have been signed. But when I was being ordered to put my unit under this command, that was an absurdity. On what basis would I do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now you're telling us something that appears to me to be very interesting. You have just told us that when this document was shown to you and you were told that the 317th Brigade needs to be subordinated to the HVO, you have just said that at your level it was not up to you to say yes or no because this would have to come from a decision by your commander-in-chief. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so. The Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina would need to make a decision to this effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your colleague Colonel Andric who tells you this, he knows there are chains of command, and when he's addressing you, is that the proper level to address this to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Colonel Andric was executing orders received from his chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Your Honours, I think I could contribute to improved understanding of this document. According to this document, no one needed to subordinate themselves to anyone. The Chief of Staff of the HVO can issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
