utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're developing a theory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I just wish to draw attention to point 7 of this decision which says that commanders of operative zones must talk to commanders of Bosnia-Herzegovina to find the best solution to establish joint commands, because as the witness said, this is a decision that had to be taken at the highest level because it entailed the reorganisation of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina consisting of the HVO and the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, yes, but in this case Colonel Siljeg spoke with the force of arms. He didn't sit down and talk about it. He spoke with the force of arms. Unfortunately, he attacked the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis, we have 10 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, in response to what you just said, "unfortunately he attacked the town," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: He attacked the town with everything he had at his disposal. And I see from these reports that what he was short of he asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you there, sir. When you say "he," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I am referring to Colonel Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when did he attack the town?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: He attacked it on the 12th of January, openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long, sir, did this attack take place?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: The attack on Gornji Vakuf lasted until it was finally halted in the second half of February. But throughout that time negotiations were conducted and attempts were made to stop the conflict. Commissions were formed after the 20th of January, but the cease-fire did not bear fruit. Then another commission was formed and two seniors officers from the 4th Corps, upon orders from General Pasalic, were sent to assist in a solution, in finding a solution. But until the truce was signed by General Petkovic and General Pasalic, and probably some other circumstances were fulfilled which I was not aware of, and this truce somehow lasted until the 20th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Brigadier Agic, at line 25 of page 91, your answer is recorded as, "He attacked the town with everything he had at his disposal." I asked you if you could please explain that and perhaps amplify what you mean by "everything he had at his disposal."

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: I repeat. When I said that he attacked with everything at his disposal, I meant that he used all available artillery that he had, howitzers, 120-millimetre mortars, 130-millimetre cannon, a VBR of 122 millimetres known as Grad, 60-millimetre mortars, 82-millimetre mortars, and finally tank units joined in as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, from which direction Gornji Vakuf was targeted by these weapons that you've just outlined?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: At the time the multiple-rocket launcher, for instance, was positioned to the right of the road before you reach the coffee bar approaching the monument. Close to him and on the other side a 203 howitzer, General Mate Sarlija from Mount Igman was positioned there. Then also I can explain in greater detail the positions. The tanks were mobile, and they were deployed as necessary. The howitzers were in the region of Mackovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Trial Chamber what was happening in the actual town of Gornji Vakuf itself in terms of any type of combat?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: The HVO prepared units for attack, the best quality ones, at least that is my opinion. The military police battalion was exerting pressure and attack on lines which was defended by the brigade police, and from the 14th or the 15th this military police battalion was joined by Mladen Naletilic, Tuta's battalion, and that is where the worst infantry combat was conducted, and also in the region of Vrse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Brigadier Agic, can you tell us if you know or if you had reports available to you what type of infantry weapons were being employed in the city of Gornji Vakuf in the middle of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: In addition to regular infantry weapons and anti-armour devices, HVO members used nitroglycerine rifles. In street combat they have a frightening effect. Fortunately, except for making a lot of noise and direct hits, they're not -- they're not that dangerous. They were used in large quantities. And later on when a truce was made in the region of the Ciganski meadows, I think they fired about a thousand of them because they had plenty of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The term nitroglycerine rifles is not commonly used in English. Can you describe what type of weapon this is?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: It's a rifle. The Western armies have an edition, and it is filled with a bullet, I think 23 calibre, and it is filled with a drum with six to eight bullets, and then it is fired like a pistol with a drum. It can be filled with helio [phoen], which is inflammable, or nitroglycerine which creates a lot of noise, a large explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: One final question, sir, before we adjourn for the evening. You've told us about meetings that took place between the HVO and the ARBiH and UNPROFOR and other internationals during the period from the 14th to the 16th of January, 1993. Did those meetings take place during cease-fires or was the fighting going on or were there lulls in the fighting during these meetings? Can you describe?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC
utterances.text: Before the 20th of January when the first truce was signed, which didn't hold, I think it was the 18th or the 19th of January, 1993, the town was visited by General Morillon, the commander of the UN forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I think the ambassador of the European Union based in Zenica, Mr. Bousseau, came to visit. I think Raymond Lee also came to UNPROFOR on that day. He was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not responsive, Your Honour. I mean, he's indicated there was fighting in the town. The question was, on the 14th, 15th where these meetings take place. Where. And I think when -- he starts with the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The question wasn't so much "where" the meetings were; the question was, was the fighting going on at the same time the meetings were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if you look at his previous testimony, he had indicated that there was fighting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On a daily basis in Gornji Vakuf while the fighting was ongoing there were negotiations in the UTL factory at the UNPROFOR headquarters in an effort to stop the fighting. Colonel Siljeg in the meantime on the ground operated militarily, and when he did something, he would say, "We will not discuss that." And he would look at his watch and say, "When the HVO captured such-and-such place." I'm saying that General Morillon came because the parties had agreed to sign a cease-fire on the 20th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to stop for today. According to my accounts, Mr. Mundis, you have used two hours, 20. How much more time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We've put the witness down for three hours, and I would expect that we would probably need that, meaning that we would need about 30 to 45 minutes tomorrow. I will do my best to reduce the number of remaining documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to make an observation, Your Honour, an observation in a way of an objection for future purposes. I don't think it's proper to have a witness take documents with him to study them overnight prior to giving testimony. Why is that? Because these documents the gentleman on almost every single occasion has indicated that he was not familiar with them. I think it taints one's memory. We don't know actually what he knew versus what he learned from the documents. I'm not suggesting anything nefarious, but I think as memories work, it does cloud the ability to distinguish what you learned the night before by reading a document versus what you remember, and I think we need to be very, very careful. I don't object to having a document shown to the witness for the first time, but to show them the night before, after the proofing session, where they know exactly where the Prosecution's story line is going, and I assume they also tell them what these nefarious Defence lawyers are going to ask about because that's how proofing normally goes on both sides. So I think we need to be careful. I would object to this practice, Your Honour, and I think one of my colleagues may join me on that issue as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you will respond to this. But what has been done would also apply to your witnesses. So when you have witnesses of the HVO, you will have dozens of documents, you'll review them the night before, and you will tell them, "Look at the documents because you'll be asked about them tomorrow." What you're criticising the Prosecution for you may be doing yourself tomorrow. Mr. Mundis, us shall response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. This is not a standard practice by any means what we've ended up with yesterday was a situation, as I've explained, where due to a number of changes that the witness wanted made to his statement we simply ran out of time to complete the proofing with the number of documents assigned. The choice would have been to delay today's hearing to continue proofing the witness or to show him the documents for the first time in the courtroom which is not, in our experience, a very productive way of going forward. So the witness was not given his homework to go and study based on the questions I'd asked him. It was simply a question of, take these remaining documents that we haven't discussed yet and have a read through them so when we completed the proofing this morning we could do so expeditiously with the limited amount of time available so that the witness then didn't have to read the document for the first time sitting in a proofing room somewhere. It was a way of simply saying, take a look at these documents tonight, we'll talk about them tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine and for the record Mr. Mundis is an honourable man and we trust him. It's just that I find it usual. This is the first time in my practice where a witness actually has taken documents to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And it was the first time in my practice as well but, again, it was because we spent a considerable period of time correcting the statement and there was simply no time left to go through the statements. The Defence will discover this as well, VWS has very strict rules about how long we can keep a witness here. They want them out of the building no later than 7.00 so that they're back at the hotel, and we have all kinds of limitations like that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you will come back tomorrow for the hearing beginning at 2.15. Of course in the meantime you will not see anyone. You are now a witness of justice. You don't "belong" to the Prosecution. You're a witness of the Court. So you will not communicate with anyone. The documents that you have, leave them here. So listen to the radio or discuss other matters this evening, because it works here, and we will meet again tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of November, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.07 p.m.,
